name: First party cookies
plain: Small name and value pairs a site stores in the browser and gets back on every request.
meaning: The base identifier of the web: a random ID in a cookie lets a site recognise a returning browser, keep a login, and join visits into one profile. It is sent automatically with every matching request, so the person never has to act.

access.persistence: Session cookie until browser closes, or up to 400 days in Chrome (cap since Chrome 104), 7 days for script set cookies in Safari
access.revocation: Clear site data, browser privacy settings

limits.headline: Can keep small notes in your browser and get them back on every visit
limits.user_action: Nothing. It happens when you visit, sign in or accept a cookie banner.
can: Send the note back with each request to its own site
Count your visits and recognize you when you return
cannot: See cookies that belong to other sites
Store much, since each cookie holds about 4 KB
Keep them after you clear cookies
Follow you across other sites on its own

story.what_it_is: Small name and value notes that a site keeps in your browser and gets back with every visit.

marketing.name: SameSite cookies explained
marketing.pitch: Google explains how sites set cookies and how browsers limit them to protect against cross site misuse.

marketing.name: HTTP cookies
marketing.pitch: Documents the small pieces of data a site stores in a browser and gets back on later requests.

story.for_you: You see it as staying logged in, a saved language and a cart that waits for you. Many sites show a cookie banner, which is about the cookies they plan to set.
story.for_makers: First party cookies keep logins, carts and settings working. Makers also use them for analytics and for remembering who you are. Third party cookies are different and are being limited.

use_cases.example: A store remembers your cart for a week so you can come back and check out.
A social site keeps you signed in so you do not enter a password each day.
A browser game keeps your player ID and best score between visits.
A site counts unique visitors by giving each browser a random ID cookie.
A site stores a click ID from an ad so it can later credit the ad for a sale.
A bank sets a short lived cookie after login and uses it to block stolen sessions.
A news site counts articles read this month to decide when to show a paywall.

technical_bounds: About 4096 bytes per cookie (name plus value)
Chrome allows roughly 180 cookies per domain and Firefox 150
Chrome caps Expires and Max-Age at 400 days
Safari ITP caps script set cookies at 7 days
SameSite=Lax is the Chrome default since Chrome 80
HttpOnly hides a cookie from scripts

abuse: Unique ID cookies joined across pages and, with sync, across sites

history.change: SameSite=Lax by default for cookies without the attribute
Expires and Max-Age capped at 400 days
ITP 2.3 capped script set cookies at 7 days (24 h when from link decorated visits)
